issues.legal_issue: The time spent in an earlier civil proceeding is excluded from limitation only when the statutory conditions for exclusion are met, including that the earlier and later proceedings concern the same matter and that the earlier proceeding failed because of a jurisdictional defect or a defect of like nature.
material_facts: The later proceeding was a suit for possession based on the claim of title to the land and the assertion that the respondents could not retain possession under the governing land law.
The earlier proceeding sought restitution because the order under which the respondents obtained possession had been reversed.
The restitution proceeding was rejected on the merits because the consolidation authorities’ decision had become final, not because the authority lacked jurisdiction or faced a like defect.
The later suit was filed beyond the prescribed limitation period; the Court assumed, in the appellants’ favour, that they had pursued the earlier proceeding diligently and in good faith.
issues.conclusion: The appellants could not exclude the time spent in the restitution proceeding because the later suit did not concern the same matter in issue and the earlier proceeding had failed on the merits rather than for a jurisdictional defect or a defect of like nature.
issues.legal_principle: Limitation Act, 1963, Section 14(1), requires due diligence, identity of the matter in issue, and good-faith prosecution of the earlier proceeding in a court unable to entertain it because of a defect of jurisdiction or other cause of a like nature. The phrase “other cause of a like nature” is read ejusdem generis with “defect of jurisdiction”: it covers a preliminary defect that, if established, makes the court incompetent to entertain the proceeding on its merits, not a failure on the merits. Explanation (C) treats misjoinder of parties or causes of action as a cause of like nature. The Court referred to India Electric Works Ltd. v. James Mantosh & Anr. as support for denying the benefit where the earlier proceeding failed on the merits.

predicates.later_suit_follows_restitution_proceedin: A party files a substantive suit after an earlier proceeding seeking restitution of property.
predicates.different_matters_in_issue: The earlier proceeding turns on whether an order was reversed or varied, while the later suit turns on the party’s substantive right to the property.
predicates.prior_proceeding_failed_on_merits: The earlier proceeding was rejected because of a determination on the merits rather than a jurisdictional or analogous preliminary defect.

issues.definition: When a substantive suit follows a restitution proceeding, concerns a different matter, and the earlier proceeding failed on the merits, the time spent in that proceeding is not excluded from limitation.

issues.legal_issue: An applicant seeking restitution must establish that the applicant lost property under a decree and that the decree was reversed, varied, modified, or set aside; the applicant need not establish title to the property in the restitution proceeding.
material_facts: The appellants sought possession through a restitution application after the order under which the respondents had obtained possession was reversed.
The restitution application did not require the appellants to prove their title or independent right to possess the land.
issues.conclusion: Restitution under Section 144 is based on the loss of property under a decree and the subsequent reversal or variation of that decree, rather than on proof of title.
issues.legal_principle: Code of Civil Procedure, Section 144, provides for restitution when a decree under which a party was made to part with property is reversed, varied, or modified, or is set aside or modified in a suit brought for that purpose. The provision embodies the equitable principle that a party should not retain an advantage obtained under a decree that is later reversed or modified.

predicates.restitution_proceeding: A party applies to the court for restoration of property through a restitution proceeding.
predicates.property_lost_under_decree: The applicant was made to part with the property under a decree.
predicates.decree_reversed_or_modified: The decree under which the applicant lost the property was later reversed, varied, modified, or set aside.

issues.definition: When a restitution applicant lost property under a decree and that decree was later reversed or modified, restitution is due without requiring proof of title.

issues.legal_issue: A final allotment made in consolidation proceedings cannot be challenged through a later civil or revenue suit concerning rights in the land or a matter that could or ought to have been addressed in those proceedings.
material_facts: The consolidation authorities allotted the disputed plots to the respondents.
The village was later denotified, and the allotment had become final.
The appellants subsequently filed a suit seeking possession and disputing the respondents’ right to retain the land.
issues.conclusion: The suit was barred because the final allotment could not be questioned in a civil or revenue court.
issues.legal_principle: Section 49 of the U.P. Consolidation of Holdings Act, 1953, bars civil and revenue courts from entertaining suits or proceedings concerning rights in land in a notified consolidation area, or other matters for which a proceeding could or ought to have been taken under that Act. Once the village was denotified and the allotment became final, the allotment could not be challenged by a later suit.

predicates.land_rights_suit: A party brings a civil or revenue suit concerning rights in land or a matter dealt with in consolidation proceedings.
predicates.consolidation_proceedings_completed: The consolidation proceedings for the relevant area have concluded.
predicates.final_land_allotment: The consolidation authorities made an allotment of the land that became final.

issues.definition: A suit concerning land rights is barred when consolidation proceedings have concluded and a final allotment covers the land.

issues.legal_issue: A cultivator who qualifies as an adhivasi under the applicable land law and has been dispossessed may seek to regain possession through the prescribed statutory application, even where another party claims bhumidar status.
material_facts: The respondents had been in possession and cultivating the land during part of the relevant agricultural year, and their names were recorded as occupants for that year.
They were dispossessed and later applied under the applicable land law to regain possession.

The Court accepted the finding that the respondents had acquired adhivasi status and were entitled to regain possession; it considered that status applicable even assuming the appellants had become bhumidars.
issues.conclusion: The respondents were adhivasis entitled to seek and regain possession through the statutory remedy.
issues.legal_principle: Section 20(b), read with Explanation I, of the U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950, supported the respondents’ adhivasi status on the facts found. The Court also relied on the statutory remedy under Section 232 of that Act for regaining possession, and noted the relevance of Section 27(1)(c) of the United Provinces Tenancy (Amendment) Act, 1947, to the respondents’ status.

predicates.possession_recorded_for_relevant_year: A cultivator’s occupancy of land during the relevant agricultural year is recorded.
predicates.cultivator_later_dispossessed: The cultivator is subsequently dispossessed of the land.
predicates.application_to_regain_possession: The dispossessed cultivator applies through the statutory process to recover possession.

issues.definition: A cultivator whose relevant-year occupancy was recorded, who was later dispossessed, and who applies through the statutory process is entitled to seek recovery of possession.
